key_points: M. R. Pai's "1971 Elections and India's Future" reads the Lok Sabha result as a personal mandate for Indira Gandhi and the collapse of the anti-Congress Democratic Front, then warns that her promised nationalisation and price-control programme risks a "Stalinist" economic dependency on the Soviet Union.

K. K. Sinha's "Election In West Bengal" traces the CPM's emergence as the dominant force of the Bengal left and Congress(J)'s consolidation as the anti-CPM rallying point, forecasting continued class warfare with the Army newly deployed to police thanas.

Writing as "Atreya", the author's "Election Trends In Tamil Nadu" attributes the DMK's landslide sweep of the assembly and Lok Sabha seats to calculated political opportunism rather than popularity, while cataloguing electoral-roll irregularities and warning the DMK against triumphalist retaliation.

An extract from the US President's Report to Congress lays out American policy toward South Asia, citing economic and family-planning aid to India and disclosing a one-time exception permitting arms sales to Pakistan.

A. B. Shah's tribute to Philip Spratt recounts the former Communist agent's journey through the Meerut Conspiracy trial to liberal humanism under M. N. Roy's influence, and the difficulty his book "Hindu Culture and Personality" faced finding an Indian publisher.

V. K. Sinha reviews Abraham Brumberg's "In Quest of Justice", tracing the post-Stalin literary "thaw" and the 1966 Siniavsky-Daniel trial as the turning point that shifted Soviet dissent from literary freedom to demands for constitutional rights.

A further review of A. G. Noorani's "India's Constitution and Politics" praises its treatment of the presidency, Cabinet system and parliamentary privileges, singling out its dispassionate debunking of communal-riot myths.
The issue also carries a tabulated results page for the 1971 Parliament and West Bengal/Tamil Nadu assembly elections, alongside the regular "With Many Voices" digest of press quotations.

Adam Adil's "Bangla Desh" surveys the outbreak of civil war after the declaration of independence under acting President Nazrul Islam, tracing West Pakistani economic and military dominance, the failed Mujib-Bhutto talks, and the army's destruction of Dacca and Chittagong.

K. K. Sinha's follow-up "Bangla Desh - Second Phase" argues Yahya Khan and Bhutto used negotiations as cover to bring in reinforcements, sets out five urgent tasks for the fledgling Bangla Desh government, and urges India to recognise it promptly.
An unsigned piece marks Novosti's tenth anniversary, describing the Soviet news agency's propaganda network and correspondents' alleged intelligence activity leading to expulsions abroad.

The "Notes" column's "Revolt in Ceylon" reads the JVP insurgency as a warning about India's own pool of unemployed educated youth, while "Electoral System" cites the 1971 results to argue India's first-past-the-post system badly distorts representation.

S. V. Raju's "Alliance That Never Was" dissects the collapse of the anti-Congress Grand Alliance of Swatantra, Congress(O), Jan Sangh and the SSP, arguing Congress dominated seats despite winning under 44% of votes because of opposition disunity.
Horst Hartmann explains West Germany's mixed-member electoral system and its five-per-cent threshold, designed as a lesson from the Weimar Republic's collapse into Nazism.
Review notices cover Solzhenitsyn's "For the Good of the Cause" as bureaucratic satire and Victor M. Fic's "The Prague Spring: 1968" as an indictment of Soviet intervention in Czechoslovakia.

A reader's letter responding to M. R. Pai's election article debates whether India's welfare state should rest on private or public enterprise, and the closing "With Many Voices" page compiles press quotations on the Bangla Desh crisis.

V. B. Karnik's "Non-Interference and Bangla Desh" argues the Panchsheel principle of non-interference has historically shielded atrocities and calls for economic sanctions against Pakistan rather than military intervention.

R. Muthuswamy's "The Quest For Peace In Mid-east" traces the Rogers Plan and Sadat's shift away from Soviet dependence, arguing reopening the Suez Canal offers the best route to a just Middle East peace.

M. R. Pai's "Planning Plans" attacks the confusion and waste of India's centralised planning, citing heavy losses at Hindustan Steel and other public-sector undertakings and warning of an eventual popular reckoning.

Ian Tickle's "The Sudan In Soviet Strategy" argues Soviet aid to General Numeiry's suppression of the southern rebellion reflects a calculated bid for Red Sea naval access rather than ideological sympathy.

Arvind A. Deshpande's "Freedom Of The Press" warns that Indira Gandhi's talk of a "committed" press threatens the ideal Nehru once championed, and reports the Working Journalists' call to place PTI and UNI under independent statutory control.

M. D. Kini reviews Kuldip Nayar's and Rajinder Puri's books on the 1969 Congress split, faulting Indira Gandhi's tactics against the "Syndicate" while judging the episode a poor reflection on Indian democratic norms.

A "Without Comment" item reproduces US Assistant Secretary of State Joseph Sisco's statement praising India's fifth national election and describing American support for East Pakistani refugee relief.
The closing "With Many Voices" page compiles press quotations on the Bangla Desh crisis, including C. Rajagopalachari questioning whether the Great Powers have abandoned South Asia to China.

M. S. Dabke's "The Budget and the Common Man" argues the 1971 budget burdens ordinary Indians through regressive indirect taxes while capital formation has fallen sharply, with barely 3.5% of revenue directed to welfare.
The Notes section treats the Bangla Desh refugee influx as an international responsibility on the model of UNRWA, and views the new PSP-SSP "Socialist Party" merger skeptically.
S. R. Mohan Das's "Labour Movement - The Future" describes INTUC, HMS and AITUC's post-election fragmentation, arguing India's intelligentsia-led unions were never rooted in genuine worker control.

S. S. Voronitsyn's "Russia: Towards Hereditary Elite" documents a widening gap between Soviet secondary graduates and university places, showing access increasingly determined by parental connections rather than merit.

Reviews cover Almond and Coleman's "The Politics of the Developing Areas" as an ambitious but geo-culturally thin comparative-politics framework, and B. K. Dutt's "Mutiny of the Innocents" as a first-hand account crediting the 1946 RIN mutiny with hastening independence.
A. Yodfat's survey of Soviet-Arab Communist Party relations shows Moscow repeatedly subordinating local Communists in Egypt, Iraq and Sudan to its state-to-state interests with Arab regimes.
A reprinted Economist item describes Chinese "freedom swimmers" fleeing to Hong Kong and harsher measures against escapers' families.
The closing "With Many Voices" page quotes Lee Kuan Yew on India and Ceylon's post-independence chaos and Minoo Masani describing himself as "always a radical, never a conservative."

S. V. Raju's "Autonomy for States?" examines the Tamil Nadu government's Rajamannar Committee report on Centre-State relations, arguing its loaded terms of reference undercut recommendations that nonetheless merit serious study, especially on finance and licensing.

V.B.K.'s "From Here and There" column welcomes Nixon's planned Peking visit while worrying it may come at India's expense, condemns continued US aid to Pakistan as "cruel and senseless", and dismisses a Bombay taxi-strike bandh as a flop.

M. R. Pai's "Black Money" traces the origins of unaccounted income to tax evasion, licence corruption and political funding, rejecting demonetisation and proposing higher exemption ceilings and lower tax rates instead.

Mohan Joshi's "Insurrection In Ceylon" reports on the JVP uprising and India's rapid military and logistic assistance to the Bandaranaike government, calling it a foreign-policy success not without risk.
A "These Things Were Happening" feature reproduces a television interview with former US Secretary of State Dean Rusk defending the conduct of the Vietnam War against Pentagon Papers criticism.

Book reviews cover Asok Chanda's "Under the Indian Sky" proposal to redraw states into linguistically homogeneous units, N. S. Gorekar's study of Persian influence on Indian languages, and Dietmar Rothermund's essays on Indian nationalism.

The closing "With Many Voices" page quotes Frank Moraes comparing Nixon to "the monkey China employed to pull its chestnuts out of the fire" and The Economist judging India "a certain loser" from the Bangladesh crisis.

Arvind A. Deshpande's "India's International Relations" reassesses non-alignment after the Indo-Soviet Treaty, arguing India should not over-invest in Moscow but pursue bilateral ties with Japan and Western Europe as a counterweight.

M. D. Kini's "Amendments And Welfare" opposes the 24th Constitution Amendment Bill and the forthcoming 25th, defending property as a fundamental right against subordination to the Directive Principles.
Writing as "Hippopotamus", "Dollar-Crisis" explains Nixon's suspension of gold convertibility as the effective end of Bretton Woods and favours floating exchange rates over new protectionism.
Charles Foley's "Conspiracy In Mexico" reports a Soviet- and North Korean-linked guerrilla plot uncovered in Mexico City, modelled on Castro's insurgency strategy and financed by bank robbery.

"Without Comment" items reprint P. Kodanda Rao's critique of the Golaknath judgment's internal contradictions and a U.S. News survey finding 16 of 23 Asian nations embroiled in Peking-instigated conflict.
G. L. Mehta's open letter, as former Indian Ambassador to the US, condemns American arms support for Pakistan's crackdown in East Pakistan as tantamount to complicity in genocide.
Reviews cover Karl Friedrich Grau's "Silesian Inferno" on Soviet atrocities against German civilians in Silesia and Satyavrata Patel's polemical "The Marxian Mirage".

The closing "With Many Voices" page quotes M. R. Masani on statism "spilling over" into the cultural sphere and multiple sources warning the Indo-Soviet Treaty could become "a millstone round the neck" of India.

Writing as "Atreya", "Take-over of Press" argues a proposed press take-over law, ostensibly targeting a "monopoly press", is designed to hand trustee control of major newspapers to Communist-aligned unions.

An editorial notice, "A Victory Of Reason", mourns the death of former Freedom First editor Raman Desai; a companion piece under "Hippopotamus" narrates the 1971 Four-Power Berlin agreement as the effective end of a quarter-century of confrontation.

A correspondent's report on a Bombay seminar of the Fundamental Rights Front, presided over by K. Subba Rao, records warnings from M. R. Masani and A. D. Gorwala that the 24th and 25th Amendments risk turning "constitutional democracy" into "constitutional despotism".
F. Hajenko's "Economic Reform In Russia" traces the Soviet reform programme's origin in declining growth and its incomplete implementation amid bureaucratic conservatism.
A "Without Comment" digest compares Chinese and Soviet military strength and catalogues Soviet-controlled Communist front organisations shaken by the invasion of Czechoslovakia.
Reviews fault Sudhir Hendre's "Hindus and Family Planning" as an unsupported anti-Muslim polemic and summarise K. R. Bhandarkar and Raja Kulkarni's book on slow computerisation in India.
A letter from S. R. Narayana Ayyar argues Centre-State disputes are manufactured by self-centred politicians rather than reflecting genuine popular division.
The closing "With Many Voices" page quotes N. A. Palkhivala on dogma as the enemy of economic wisdom and C. Rajagopalachari praising the international standing the Indo-Soviet Treaty gave India.

V. B. Karnik's "Ballots and Bullets" attacks the Communist Party (Right)'s declared combination of electoral and revolutionary tactics as self-contradictory and warns Congress against cultivating ties with it.
A. G. Mulgaokar's "Nixon - Denying His Country's History" accuses Nixon of betraying America's revolutionary heritage by continuing to arm Yahya Khan's regime during the Bangladesh crisis.

Writing as "Atreya", "Is Parliament Redundant for Socialism?" criticises the government's growing reliance on Ordinances rather than parliamentary legislation, faulting trade unions for compounding the trend.
Adam Adil's "Bangla Desh" reports India's mounting refugee burden and continued US arms sales to Pakistan, arguing the Indo-Soviet Treaty has already deterred Pakistani war rhetoric.
A report on the Liberal International's Zurich Congress records resolutions on the East Bengal refugee crisis and on threats to Indian press freedom from proposed Companies Act amendments.
K. K. Sinha's "Transformation Of Congress In W. Bengal" credits the Chhatra Parishad and Yuva Congress youth organisations for Congress(R)'s doubled seat count in the March 1971 state election.

Reviews cover T. V. Kunhi Krishnan's biography of Y. B. Chavan and U. R. Rao's reminiscences of Gandhi, while "Saadi"'s satirical "Mock Air Raid" recounts a farcically bungled Bombay civil-defence exercise.

A Minority Rights Group report on Soviet treatment of the Crimean Tatars and Volga Germans, and N. J. Tavaria's bitter letter on the decline of Indo-US relations, round out an issue closing with the usual "With Many Voices" digest.

V. B. Karnik's "Clouds of War" surveys the India-Pakistan standoff on the eve of war, arguing conflict will not solve the Bangla Desh refugee crisis and urging international pressure toward a negotiated settlement.
An editorial tribute mourns Freedom First correspondent K. K. Sinha, while a report on an Indian Liberal Group seminar records unanimous opposition to proposed press-ownership-diffusion legislation.
Unsigned "Notes" condemn Ruling Congress violence in Delhi, the year-long Customs delay in releasing Ved Mehta's "Portrait of India", and cautiously welcome signs of a Sino-Indian thaw.
R. Muthuswamy's "C.P.M. In Wilderness" analyses the party's isolation ahead of its Madurai congress and its double-faced strategy of public moderation alongside cadre-driven agitation.

M. R. Masani's "The End Of The U.N.?" attacks the expulsion of Taiwan and admission of Communist China as a moral and strategic catastrophe comparable to the League of Nations' collapse over Abyssinia.
An extract from an Observer interview with World Bank president Robert McNamara warns developing-world population could reach 14,500 million even under an optimistic fertility scenario.
A. B. Shah's "The Meaning Of Jodhpur" uses the attack on Vice-Chancellor V. V. John to argue for financially independent universities insulated from populist and political pressure.

Abraham Brumberg reviews Andrei Amalrik's "Involuntary Journey to Siberia" on rural Soviet servitude, and a further review recalls Gandhi's humility through U. R. Rao's reminiscences, while a reader's letter on Indo-US relations and "With Many Voices" close the issue.

M. R. Masani's "Rededication" editorial marks Freedom First's approaching twentieth year, warns of a "Marxist counter-revolution" eroding civil liberties, and announces Masani's resumption of the editorship from V. B. Karnik.

The "Notes" column reads Maharashtra minister A. R. Antulay's land-ceiling remarks as an admission that full land nationalisation is the real Congress goal, and mocks Galbraith's admitted planning errors.
A. G. Noorani's "On Pamphleteering" laments the decline of committed Indian political writing since the era of Naoroji, Tilak and the Congress Socialist Party generation.
J. R. Patel profiles veteran editor A. D. Gorwala, tracing his ICS career, his 1948 resignation over food-price decontrol, and his uneconomically priced weekly Opinion.

N. L. Panjwani's "Education Should Invade Politics" rejects the claim that politics has newly "invaded" education, arguing the system has always been shaped by the country's political and economic structure.
Brigadier J. P. Dalvi's "Outward Bound" describes the Leslie Sawhny Programme's incorporation of UK-style physical leadership training for youth and trade-union leaders.

Geeta Doctor reviews an Elphinstone College production of Tendulkar's "Silence! The Court Is in Session!", and further reviews cover Nari Rustomji's Northeast-frontier memoir and a study of the Sarvodaya movement's Bhoodan-Gramdan leadership.

B. K. Nehru's Madon Memorial Lecture, "First Priority", argues mass unemployment must override every other policy objective, projecting 37 million unemployed by 1980 and criticising government practices that manufacture false employment.
The "Notes" column welcomes Bangladesh's liberation while criticising Indira Gandhi's reversal on Constitution Amendment concessions and the detention of Current editor D. F. Karaka.
Mehra Masani's "AIR" argues All India Radio remains anomalous among democracies in lacking BBC-style autonomy, rebutting government objections to implementing the Chanda Committee's recommendations.

S. V. Raju's "The U.N. Vote" reads India's near-total isolation in the December 1971 ceasefire vote as evidence the Indo-Soviet Treaty destroyed its non-aligned credibility, calling for an "agonising reappraisal" of foreign policy.
Richard Brookhiser offers a psychological portrait of Nixon as a political "Romantic" ahead of his China trip, comparing him to Neville Chamberlain and Czar Alexander I at Tilsit.

A translated Soviet "magnitizdat" protest ballad by Mikhail Nozhkin satirises the hypocrisy of a privileged Soviet "New Class", with an editorial note drawing a parallel to India's own emerging elite.
Aziz Madni reviews "Shadow of the Bear" on the Indo-Soviet Treaty's implications, and the closing "With Many Voices" page compiles quotations on the Bangladesh war's diplomatic fallout.

Joan Contractor's "Misfortunes of a Bombay University Drop-Out" recounts an American graduate student's disillusioning month at Bombay University, contrasting its fragmented lecture system with American continuity.

The "Notes" column praises Governor Dharma Vira for resisting Central pressure, reports the founding of the National Union of Journalists under Frank Moraes, and criticises the Prime Minister's demand that states "fall in line" with the Centre.

A. G. Noorani's "The Alternatives in Kashmir" surveys decades of rigged Kashmir elections and the externment of Plebiscite Front leaders, criticising the Front for failing to develop a democratic alternative once the plebiscite became moot.
R. Hawkins's "'Nationalised' Textbooks" argues against centralised textbook production, proposing competing series and standard-setting committees instead.
Nissim Ezekiel reviews the Medvedev brothers' "A Question of Madness" on Zhores Medvedev's psychiatric detention for dissent, framing Soviet psychiatric persecution as "ideological madness".
A review of Robert Conquest's "Where Marx Went Wrong" questions Conquest's thesis that Marx's system was merely corrupted by successors, while Geeta Doctor surveys Bombay's gallery scene.

An open letter from Anya Nya commander Colonel Joseph Lagu appeals to the OAU over alleged mass killing of Bantus in Southern Sudan, and a letter from J. B. H. Wadia credits M. N. Roy's pioneering pamphleteering legacy.

Suzanne Labin's "Goa: The End of the Hashish Trail" reports on the hippie colony at Kalengute beach, describing physical deterioration among young Western drug users alongside the local cottage economy it has sustained.
M. R. Masani's editorial "The Retreat From Peking" calls Nixon's China visit a "moment of infamy" that betrayed Taiwan and Tibet's claims to self-determination for no reciprocal concession.
A. G. Noorani's "The Brezhnev Plan Revisited" argues Moscow's undisclosed Asian collective-security proposal is aimed at containing China despite persistent denials.
S. K. Rau recounts the formation of the National Union of Journalists (India) as a revolt against the politically infiltrated Indian Federation of Working Journalists.
Writing as "Hippopotamus", "Why Not Peace?" defends Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik treaties against critics who call them premature or an overestimation of German leverage.
Anil C. Dharker reviews William F. Buckley's diary-memoir "Cruising Speed", pushing back on Buckley's argument that majority freedom sometimes requires suppressing minorities.
Geeta Doctor reviews Alyque Padamsee's staging of Gurcharan Das's play "Mira" as a visually striking "20th century look at the phenomenon of sainthood".
M. R. Masani's "Foreign Aid Must Go" welcomes the suspension of US aid to India as a blessing in disguise, arguing government-to-government aid entrenches statism and bureaucratic power.
The "Notes" column details allegations of vote-rigging in the March 1972 state elections and criticises India's turn to Soviet computer collaboration over more advanced American technology.
Manjula Padmanabhan introduces kinesics, or body language, surveying gestures said to reveal unconscious defensiveness and cross-cultural differences in touch norms.

S. V. Raju's "Democracy Without Brakes" argues Congress's state-election landslide reflected superior financing and a divided opposition rather than genuine mandate, since it won only 44.64% of the vote but 71% of seats.
An unsigned "Tale of a Glove" satirises Soviet bureaucratic shortages through the story of a war-wounded pensioner's months-long failed search for gloves.
A translated Indira Gandhi-Gaddafi correspondence over the 1971 war shows Gaddafi rejecting Indian appeals and accusing India of Soviet collusion.

Farok Contractor reviews Germaine Greer's "The Female Eunuch" as a brilliant if occasionally dubious critique of sociologically conditioned femininity, and readers' letters debate Bombay University and constitutional federalism.

Writing as "Martial", the lead essay criticises Indira Gandhi's uncritical adoption of Pakistani economist Mahbub ul Haq's "employment-oriented" development ideas as collectivism dressed as novel economics.

The "Notes" column treats Kwame Nkrumah's fall as a cautionary tale about charismatic socialist dictators and reports USIA Director Frank Shakespeare's admission that the US is losing the Cold War propaganda struggle.
A. G. Noorani's "How Indian the Ocean?" surveys expanding US and Soviet naval presence in the Indian Ocean, criticising India's incoherent, rhetoric-heavy policy toward the region.
James Burnham's "What Makes Jack Anderson Tick?" analyses the motives behind leak-driven journalism under Nixon and proposes automatic declassification reform.
V. V. John's "The Crisis in Higher Education" argues Indian colleges fail to intellectually challenge students, faulting the Gajendragadkar Committee for misdiagnosing unrest as a governance problem.

Sidney Hook's "Authority and Democracy in the University" distinguishes domains of university authority, arguing faculty control over curriculum should remain near-absolute against "student power" demands.
Reviews cover J. R. Patel's harsh notice of Vinod Mehta's "Bombay: A Private View" and Nitin G. Raut's favourable notices of two books on Israel and the Arab-Israeli conflict.
Vrunda Moghe's "The Helpless Supervisor" recounts rampant, organised cheating she witnessed as a Bombay University exam supervisor, and the hostility her attempts at discipline provoked.

The editorial column assesses the Nixon-Moscow summit as producing little beyond a tactical truce, citing a Senate study claiming the Soviets violated 24 of 25 past agreements, and warns of a Communist "take-over" step in Orissa.
Sharu S. Rangnekar's "Slow Scientists and Fast Machines" criticises the glacial, committee-bound Electronics Commission for holding back India's fledgling computer industry.
R. K. Narayan's satirical "Music and the Fifty-five Year Plan" imagines Indian classical and light music nationalised under bureaucratic quotas and inspectors.
A. G. Noorani's review of Henry Cecil's Hamlyn Lectures contrasts British public scrutiny of judges with the stagnant salary and declining governmental respect facing Indian judges.
Anil Dharkar reviews the Daedalus collection "Philosophers and Kings", dwelling on Erik Erikson's psychoanalytic essay on the origins of Gandhi's non-violence.

A "Broken Pledges" tabulation catalogues alleged Soviet violations of US-Soviet summit agreements since 1943, and the closing "With Many Voices" page quotes Djilas on socialist leaders' abuse of nationalised property.
A. G. Noorani's "Breakthrough at Simla?" defends the Simla Agreement between Indira Gandhi and Bhutto as a durable, non-punitive bilateral settlement rather than a Versailles-style diktat.

The "Notes" column covers J.P. Narayan's clash with Madhya Pradesh's Chief Minister over dacoit surrenders, scepticism about a McGovern presidency, and the mysterious disappearance of scientist Zhores Medvedev.

Dharma Vira's "Leadership in Administration" contrasts pre-independence administrative decisiveness with post-independence drift, warning that demands for civil-servant "commitment" would destroy service neutrality.
Geeta Doctor's "A Lament for Madras" mourns the vanished character of the old city under urban growth, citing declining cleanliness and haphazard planning of the Marina Beach.
Steven J. Staats's "Corruption in the Soviet Union" argues corruption, via mechanisms like blat and the tolkach, is structurally integral to the Soviet command economy rather than an aberration.
Dinesh Kale reviews William J. Barnds's "India, Pakistan and the Great Powers", crediting it as a perceptive account that concludes US arms aid to the subcontinent has failed.
Film reviews cover "Dirty Harry" and V. Shantaram's "Pinjra", and the closing "With Many Voices" page quotes C. B. Irani on elected tyranny and Shimon Peres on freedom versus equality.

M. R. Masani's "Happy Anniversary" uses his own censored All India Radio interview to indict twenty-five years of governmental centralisation on the Independence Silver Jubilee, crediting Nehru's restraint for surviving democratic dialogue.
The "Notes" column warns that exchange controls, visa denials and a threatened withdrawal from copyright conventions amount to a new curtain on India's intellectual contact with the West.
Geeta Doctor's "The Hard Pressed Students" surveys new Bombay college magazines and recounts the unjust suppression of the independent magazine Experiment over its frank content.

A. G. Noorani's "The P.M., Dr. Faridi & Aligarh" documents Communist inroads at Aligarh Muslim University and Dr. A. J. Faridi's diary of pre-election autonomy assurances from Indira Gandhi that were never honoured.

Prof. F. A. Mechery's "Kerala: Politics vs. Education" analyses the standoff between private college managements and the state government over fee unification, exploited by every major political party.

Zarin Minocher-Homji's "English and the Indian Theatre" argues Indian plays performed in English ring false because the language is not the natural idiom of the country's socially marginal characters.
The closing "With Many Voices" page quotes J. R. D. Tata on government's concentration of economic power alongside remarks from Indira Gandhi and George Wallace.
J. R. Patel's "When Did Elizabeth Die?" is a wry travelogue of the hippie trail at Calangute and Anjuna, closing on a hippie's overdose death passing unremarked among her peers.

The "Notes" column welcomes the new Farmers' Federation of India against land-reform legislation, mocks the naming of Arunachal Pradesh's capital "Indira Giri", and criticises Delhi's diplomatic warmth toward Idi Amin.
Chitra Sen's "Numerically Speaking" introduces the Möbius strip and Klein bottle before turning to very large numbers and mathematics' influence on aesthetics.
A reader's letter from Dinesh C. Kale criticises proposed amendments empowering government to cancel mining leases at will, warning it would deter investment in dependent industries.
A satirical poem, "My Babujee Days", lampoons the cost and stage-managed disruption of a prime-ministerial visit to IIT Powai's convocation.

Anil Dharker reviews Richard H. Solomon's study of Mao's revolution as a struggle against Confucian filial piety, and Sujata Manohar reviews a compiled volume on the 24th and 25th Constitution Amendment Bills.
M. P. Appachu reviews Suraj Bhan Agrawal's statistical study of Indian price trends, and Alan Ross's poem "Yogis at Chowpatty Beach" closes the issue's cultural content before "With Many Voices".
M. R. Masani's editorial welcomes Nixon's re-election as a rejection of isolationism, while criticising the draft Vietnam peace agreement for allowing North Vietnamese troops to remain in the South.
The "Notes" column praises the Supreme Court's ruling striking down the government's newsprint policy, credits N. A. Palkhivala's advocacy, and reports Congress's loss in an Ahmedabad by-election.
A. G. Noorani's "Ourselves and China" argues India's exclusive reliance on Russia is leaving it isolated from China, the US and Pakistan, urging deliberate rapprochement.
An unsigned item reports the government's ban on exporting Peter Sagar's "Moscow's Hand in India", which documented Soviet propaganda channelled through the CPI's press service.
Geeta Doctor's "For Admissions, Come September" satirises the anxieties of Bombay school admissions and parents' reliance on influence.
The Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom's biennial resolutions, reprinted in full, condemn restrictions on academic foreign travel and press-freedom violations in West Bengal and Manipur.

Deepa Awal's "A General Theory" parodies Keynesian economics to explain student unrest, and Hardayal Singh reviews Prakash Tandon's memoir "Beyond Punjab" on job discrimination facing Indian managers.
J. R. Patel's "High Tide at Bandra Beach" satirises a middle-class protest against a proposed bank training institute, mocking the demonstrators' performative radicalism.

The "Notes" column compares Allende's Chile to Indira Gandhi's Congress as governments resting on thin democratic mandates, and mocks the renaming of colonial-era roads after obscure contemporary figures.
A. G. Noorani's "A Kashmir-Hyderabad Barter?" finds President Bhutto's claim of a 1947 Patel offer factually wrong, tracing the actual documented record of failed plebiscite negotiations.
Farok Contractor's skeptical account of the Asia '72 trade fair finds neglected foreign pavilions and domestic crowds treating it as cheap entertainment rather than genuine trade.
James Burnham criticises Nixon's billion-dollar grain and technology deal with the Soviet Union as strengthening an adversarial regime for dubious returns.
Geeta Doctor profiles playwright Girish Karnad through his newly published play "Tughlaq", and Kamla Chowdhry reviews a seminar volume on the crisis in higher education.

A. Chatterjee reviews A. K. Warder's survey of Indian historiography, and a Swiss Press Review piece on Peter Sager's banned book on Soviet infiltration of the Indian press closes alongside "With Many Voices".
S. V. Raju's tribute "'Carry On,' said Rajaji" recounts C. Rajagopalachari's founding of the Swatantra Party with Masani and his final instruction to keep the party's old guard together.
An editorial report on M. R. Masani's six-day visit to South Vietnam describes his helicopter flight to besieged An Loc and his impression of "stability, strength and high morale".
Mani Meherhomji's "Stranger In The Night" is an as-told-to account of an aging Bombay prostitute's decades in the trade and her eventual retreat from it for her daughter's sake.
A. Chatterjee's "Crackdown on Dissent in Russia" surveys Soviet repression built around Natalia Gorbanevskaya's account of the 1968 Red Square protest and its dissidents' psychiatric detention.
Leslie Daniel's "Encore for Malavli" assesses the Malavli Youth Festival as an organisational success that misjudged youth appetite for lectures over music and freedom from supervision.
Geeta Doctor reviews Girish Karnad's play "Hayavadana" as a brilliant if structurally uneven production, criticising Karnad's treatment of the character Padmini.
A. G. Noorani reviews J. Bernard Hutton's "The Subverters of Liberty" as an unverifiable "parody of Communist plots a Communist might write".

B. Ratnasabhapati's "Andhra in Ferment" reports on the Telangana-Andhra bifurcation agitation following the Mulki Rules judgment, describing CRP firings that killed over 300 and the collapse of Delhi's authority in the state.
The "Notes" column criticises continued detention of Pakistani POWs and covers factional maneuvering inside the Jana Sangh, Swatantra Party and the Orissa "Pragati" alliance rebuffed by J.P. Narayan.
A blind M.A. student, Raghunath Rakibe, describes the social neglect and lack of vocational opportunity facing India's blind population, calling for enforceable employment rights.
A report on the Liberal International's Jerusalem Executive Council meeting covers its condemnation of Jewish persecution in the USSR and the expulsion of Asians from Uganda.
Geeta Doctor's comic account of a Test match at Brabourne Stadium satirises the quasi-religious devotion of Indian cricket fans.
Nissim Ezekiel critiques Suzanne Labin's anti-hippie polemic "Hippies, Drugs and Promiscuity" as fundamentally unsound despite a legitimate case against drug dependence.

J. R. Patel reviews Vijay Tendulkar's "Sakharam Binder", arguing its commercial success owed more to an obscenity prosecution than to artistic merit, while R. K. Laxman and A. H. Desai review books on workaholism and Renaissance erotica.

M. R. Masani's "The True Liberal" defends classical liberalism against its inversion in American usage, arguing the Swatantra Party represents authentic liberalism despite being called "conservative" in India.
The "Notes" column warns a proposed State Trading Corporation monopoly on book imports threatens literary censorship, and cites a study finding roughly a million people in Soviet forced-labour camps.
Bhanu Pratap Singh's "For Farm and Freedom" attacks Indira Gandhi's land-ceiling policy as economically incoherent and a covert step toward Soviet-style agricultural collectivisation.
An unsigned editorial, "The Budget of an Ignoramus", excoriates Finance Minister Y. B. Chavan's 1973-74 budget for escalating deficits despite three years of heavy fresh taxation.
A. G. Noorani reviews Piloo Mody's biography of Bhutto, "Zulfi — My Friend", finding it warm but factually uncritical on the Pakistan break-up.
Manjula Padmanabhan reviews Sasti Brata's novel "Confessions of an Indian Woman Eater" as derivative and lacking genuine candour.
A wire filler recounts a Soviet bureaucratic mix-up distributing coffee as fertiliser, and a reader's letter disputes claims of indiscriminate American bombing of North Vietnam.
M. R. Masani's "The Dangerous Years" surveys India's economic outlook, blaming the government's drift toward a "monopolist and Marxist" society and setting out a seven-point liberal reform programme.

Vrunda Moghe's investigative piece estimates the cost of detaining Pakistani POWs at roughly Rs. 19.5 crores over thirteen months, questioning whether prolonged detention is worth its diplomatic cost.
A reprinted press report covers Masani's address to the Swatantra Party's Sixth National Convention, rebuking the Orissa unit for aligning with Biju Patnaik.

David Rees reports an international committee's finding of over a million prisoners across roughly a thousand Soviet forced-labour camps, including the case of samizdat editor Yury Galanskov's death in custody.
Bertram D. Wolfe's "The Nature of Totalitarianism" defines totalitarianism as the claim that party and State are coextensive with society, denying autonomy to unions, churches and individuals.
Geeta Doctor reviews a Theatre Group staging of Pinter's "The Birthday Party" and, separately, Arthur Koestler's novel "The Call-Girls".
K. Vasudeva Rao reviews Jean-François Revel's "Without Marx or Jesus", crediting its rebuttal of European myths about America while faulting its own utopian prescriptions.

M. R. Masani's "Freedom Is Indivisible" reads the supersession of three Supreme Court judges as part of a sustained Congress-Communist assault on institutions, alongside bank nationalisation and the Indo-Soviet Treaty.
A reprinted extract, "How Beria Died", recounts Khrushchev's account of Beria's summary execution, placed as an ironic counterpoint to the judiciary editorial.
The "Notes" column draws lessons from Watergate on the value of a free press and independent judiciary, and reports a sharp fall in Indira Gandhi's popularity per opinion polling.
V. B. Karnik's "What Price Afro-Asian Solidarity?" reports a former secretary's disclosures that the All India Peace Council was run as a Soviet-financed racket by a Communist Party faction.
A. G. Noorani's "Nehru and Patel" reviews Volume IV of Patel's correspondence, arguing Patel was blind to Hindu communalism while Nehru was blind to the Communist danger.
Geeta Doctor's "The Road to Matheran" recounts a toy-train family holiday and local opposition to a proposed motor road into the hill station.
Reviews cover a seminar volume on India's world role, faulted for producing vague political comment, and Alvin Toffler's "Future Shock" on society's struggle to keep pace with accelerating change.

A translated Loksatta report accuses Union Labour Minister Raghunath Reddy, a former Communist, of interfering in Maharashtra industrial disputes at Voltas, Indian Explosives and Indian Drugs and Pharmaceuticals to favour striking unions.
The "Notes" column welcomes Ronald Reagan's proposed California tax ceiling, marks Adam Smith's 250th birth anniversary, and mocks the diplomatic slight given to Ambassador T. N. Kaul in Washington.
S. V. Raju's "A Tale of Two Bandhs and a Half" satirises Bombay's rival May 1973 bandhs by Communist unions and George Fernandes, concluding neither delivered relief to the drought-hit population.
Freedom First publishes as a documentary exclusive Andrei Sakharov's 1972 Postscript to his Memorandum to Brezhnev, indicting Soviet apathy, psychiatric persecution of dissidents and militarisation.

Joan Contractor reviews Arthur Miller's Collected Plays, tracing a recurring pattern of ordinary heroes achieving tragic stature through free will, and M. R. Pai reviews Benedict Costa's polemic on India's "socialist princes".
Letters debate the June "Freedom is Indivisible" editorial's charge of a press "conspiracy of silence" and a review of a seminar volume on India's Vietnam policy.
A short item juxtaposes Gustav Husak's 1968 denial and 1971 thanks to the CPSU over the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia, closing before "With Many Voices".
A joint statement by Jayaprakash Narayan and M. R. Masani protests the arrest of Acharya Kripalani in Haryana as symptomatic of growing intolerance of dissent.
A. G. Noorani's "The Judiciary - U.K. and U.S. Models" compares the two constitutional systems, concluding India's judiciary carries a heavier burden given its shallower democratic tradition.
The "Notes" column criticises the elevation of former Communist minister V. R. Krishna Iyer to the Supreme Court as "packing the court" and attacks a rising personality cult around Indira Gandhi.
Brian Crozier's "Such Men Are Dangerous" argues Nixon-Brezhnev detente is a dangerous illusion given continuing Soviet propaganda, subversion and support for revolutionary movements abroad.
Manjula Padmanabhan recounts holding her first poster exhibition on a Bombay pavement outside the Jehangir Art Gallery.
Geeta Doctor reviews "The Position of Women in India", and Geoffrey Noronha reviews Phillip Darby's study of British defence policy east of Suez.
A heated exchange of letters between U. H. Easwarasarma and A. G. Noorani revisits whether Sardar Patel held communal bias against Muslims in 1947.
Geeta Doctor's "Much Ado About Nothing" argues Indian anxiety over Iran's rise is overblown, since India's own military strength exceeds Iran's and Pakistan's combined.
An unsigned analysis examines whether India should join Comecon, concluding from trade and growth statistics that the bloc is an economically inefficient vehicle for Soviet primacy.

L. H. Gann's "Neo-Colonialism and the 'New Class'" challenges dependency-theory claims with investment data, arguing neo-colonialism theory chiefly serves a new post-colonial administrative elite's material interests.
The "Between You & Me" column criticises price controls and a controversy over Advocate-General H. M. Seervai's lecture being co-opted by Communist sympathisers.
M. G. Bailur harshly reviews M. Chalapathi Rau's official Nehru biography as a poorly written "tourist's-guide" that reveals more about the author's vanity than his subject.
A brief review praises Sharu Rangnekar's "In the Wonderland of Indian Managers" for its satirical treatment of feudalism and nepotism in Indian management.
Manjula Padmanabhan reviews the Bombay production of "Godspell", finding its first half fully successful but its solemn second half less coherent.
Extracts from a September 1973 Solzhenitsyn interview insist one determined conscience can resist an oppressive state, citing the persecution of Andrei Amalrik and General Grigorenko.
The "Notes" column surveys renewed Stalinist-style repression, celebrates South Vietnam's Senate election under President Thieu, and criticises India's cap on visiting American scholars.
A translated samizdat programme document from the underground journal "The Sower" calls for a Soviet liberal opposition party built on scientific-democratic management and market-oriented reform.
International PEN's protest, signed by Heinrich Böll and David Carver, condemns Andrei Amalrik's renewed sentence as a contradiction of detente.
A reprinted Economist item, "A War Worth Fighting", defends continued American involvement in Vietnam as a defence of South Vietnamese pluralism against one-party rule.
Manjula Padmanabhan profiles envelope-collage artist Raobail, and Sujata Manohar reviews "A Judiciary Made to Measure" on the Supreme Court supersession protests.
Mehra Masani reviews E. N. Mangat Rai's memoir "Commitment My Style", focusing on its portrait of Punjab Chief Minister Pratap Singh Kairon's centralising, fear-inducing administration.

Manohar Malgonkar's "Eleven Years to Go?" reviews "Justice—Communist Style", using essays by Masani, Noorani, Jethmalani and Wolfe to argue the April 1973 judicial supersession signals a drift toward party-loyal courts.
Geeta Doctor's "Thailand's Revolution" traces the country's history of strongman rule since 1932 and the distinctively student-led 1973 uprising that toppled Field Marshal Thanom's regime.
Israeli minister Moshe Kol's open letter rebukes European Liberal International leaders for their silence during the Yom Kippur War, except for Willy Brandt.

Sheila Sumant's "The Controversial U.N. Resolution 242" analyses the legal ambiguity between the resolution's English and French versions on Israeli withdrawal, favouring the English working-draft interpretation.

Short items cover Amnesty International's global anti-torture campaign, finding 63 of 139 countries surveyed reportedly practise it, and Soviet-style low-level corruption toward foreign businesspeople.
S. V. Raju reviews Bimanesh Chatterjee's anecdotal memoir "Thousand Days with Rajaji", and S. P. Aiyar reviews two books on the judicial supersession crisis, including K. S. Hegde's own account.

A further review of Karl Kaiser's "Europe and United States" summarises strained transatlantic relations following Vietnam and the declining dollar, and the closing "With Many Voices" page compiles quotations on the October 1973 West Asian war.
